## Why the 8,000-character limit exists — operator context

**The limit is a load-bearing architectural decision, not an arbitrary style rule.** It was
introduced to address a chronic problem: ticket size exceeding the **completion verifier's context
window**. An oversized description does not merely make review slower — it can exceed what the
verifier can read, at which point the gate that is supposed to confirm the work degrades or fails.

This matters to how this ticket is implemented, in three ways.

### 1. The limit must not move — and the ACs already say so

The acceptance criteria state that the 8,000-character limit is UNCHANGED and that raising it does
not satisfy them. That constraint now has its reason attached: raising the limit would reintroduce
the failure it was created to prevent, in a gate whose whole purpose is to verify completion. Anyone
picking this up should treat "just raise the cap" as foreclosed, not merely out of scope.

### 2. The coaching must not over-correct into UNDER-describing

The remedy for over-length is concision, and concision has a failure mode of its own. A description
stripped of the context needed to understand the work produces a plan a reviewer cannot evaluate and
a verifier cannot check — which fails the same gate from the opposite direction.

So the message must not simply say "be shorter". The distinction it needs to teach is between:

- **context that must stay** — the problem, why it matters, the constraints the work must respect,
  the acceptance criteria and how each will be evidenced. A reader who has never seen the ticket
  should be able to understand and evaluate the plan from the description alone.
- **narration that should move** — conversational progression, investigation history, method
  discussion, rationale for choices already made, and the running account of how the author arrived
  at the plan. That material is valuable and should be preserved in ticket **comments** or a
  **session log**, where it stays discoverable without consuming the verifier's budget.

The failing description that prompted this ticket was 105 lines of narration around 14 acceptance
criteria; relocating the narration cost nothing in comprehensibility and left 44% headroom. That is
the shape of the correct fix, and it is worth stating in the message as the distinction rather than
as a word count.

### 3. It suggests where the coaching should point

Because the limit protects a downstream consumer rather than expressing a preference, the guidance
belongs with the existing authoring guidance rather than as free-floating advice. `rebar explain
plan` / `src/rebar/_guides/writing-a-passing-plan.md` is the natural home, and the message should
point there rather than restate it — otherwise the advice and the guide can drift apart, which is
the same duplication hazard that produced two other bugs in this store today.
